A control room runs around the clock, and its ambient lighting is not constant: bright during day operations, dimmed at night to reduce fatigue. Displays must remain legible and comfortable across that range without ever changing what a color means. Kronos L6 supports light and dark presentations of the same interface, tied to a stable color grammar so a hue's meaning is invariant even as its rendering adapts to the room.

Contrast is maintained against whatever the ambient condition is: a dark theme for dimmed night operation keeps the alert palette distinct and the confidence hatching visible; a light theme for bright conditions does the same. The reserved alert colors are chosen to remain unmistakable in both themes, because an alarm that washes out under one lighting condition is a latent failure. Type and glyph contrast are checked against accessibility thresholds in both themes and at each viewing distance.
Light and dark presentations of one interface, same semantics
Alert palette remains distinct in both themes and off-angle on the wall
Confidence hatching and redundant cues survive the theme switch
Brightness tuned to reduce night-shift fatigue without losing contrast
Theme change never re-maps a color's meaning

Night-shift fatigue degrades vigilance, which is exactly when the interface must work hardest to re-engage attention. Dimmable, low-glare presentation reduces the eye strain that accelerates fatigue, while the predictive shadow and precursor cues carry the load of re-engaging a tiring operator before an event. Theming is therefore not cosmetic; it is part of keeping operators effective through the hours when they are most vulnerable.

Theming sits on top of the color grammar and is held to the accessibility bar in every theme. It applies uniformly to consoles, the video wall, and mobile views so the crew never faces inconsistent renderings of the same truth.

title: Diagnostic Health Mosaic
lede: A single glanceable map of the 60+ diagnostic ports — which are healthy, degraded, dead, or imputed — because everything the operator trusts rests on this.
body: The foundation under every other number

Every estimate, KPI, and forecast on every L6 surface ultimately rests on the diagnostics feeding the twin. If an operator does not know which sensors are healthy, they cannot properly weight anything downstream. The diagnostic health mosaic is a compact map of the machine's 60+ diagnostic ports — Mirnov coils, flux loops, interferometry, Thomson scattering, neutron detectors, REBCO strain gauges, and more — each colored by health so the whole measurement front is readable at a glance.
noisy or drifting; reduced weight, wider bands
no signal; masked, excluded from estimates
reconstructed by the GNN from neighbors; flagged everywhere

Fusion diagnostics degrade under neutron and thermal load, so this map is dynamic and consequential. When a Mirnov coil drops and the GNN imputes it, the mosaic shows the port as imputed, and that state propagates: the equilibrium estimate's provenance names the imputation, its confidence widens, and the affected overlay region shows hatching. The mosaic is where the operator first sees the cause of a confidence change elsewhere.

The mosaic shows not only current state but degradation trend, so an operator can see a diagnostic drifting toward failure and plan around it before it is lost mid-shot. Calibration-drift tracking feeds this view, distinguishing a genuine physics change from an instrument going out of calibration. For both machines, sustained diagnostic-availability is a first-order KPI precisely because it gates trust in everything else.

The mosaic is the operator-facing face of signal validation and GNN imputation from L2/L3, and it directly drives confidence and provenance and the hatching in the 3D overlay. Its availability metric appears on the dashboards.

title: Out-of-Distribution Signaling to Operators
lede: The single most important trust signal: telling the operator plainly when the machine has entered a regime the AI was never trained on.
body: When the model is out of its depth

An AI model is reliable inside the regime it was trained on and unreliable — often confidently so — outside it. For machines still in design and simulation and heading toward first-of-a-kind first tritium (~2030), operators will inevitably push into states no training set covered. The most important thing L6 can tell an operator is: the AI is now extrapolating beyond what it knows. Out-of-distribution (OOD) signaling makes that explicit rather than leaving the operator to discover it through a bad recommendation.
How OOD is detected and shown

Each model reports an OOD score — how far the current input is from its training distribution — using density estimates, ensemble disagreement, or reconstruction error. When the score crosses a threshold, the affected estimate's provenance badge flips its in-distribution flag, its confidence widens, and any recommendation built on it is explicitly de-weighted. On the 3D overlay, OOD regions are marked distinctly from merely low-confidence ones, because the operator's response differs: low confidence means noisy; OOD means untrusted.

def ood_flag(x, model):
    epi   = ensemble_disagreement(x, model)     # members diverge off-distribution
    dens  = model.density_estimate(x)           # low density -> unfamiliar input
    recon = model.reconstruction_error(x)       # autoencoder-style novelty
    score = combine(epi, 1.0 - dens, recon)
    return score > OOD_THRESHOLD                 # -> badge flips, confidence widens

OOD is a cue to shift weight from the AI toward first-principles physics and human judgment, and often to lower the automation level. The interface actively suggests this: when a safety-relevant loop's model goes OOD, the trust-and-override surface recommends more human involvement, and the copilot flags that its reasoning is now less grounded. This is the honest posture the whole stack takes — the AI advises within what it knows and says so clearly when it doesn't.
OOD signaling is the sharp edge of uncertainty visualization and the provenance badges, and it directly shapes trust and override decisions during novel operation.

title: First-Out and Root-Cause Presentation
lede: In a cascade, showing the first alarm to fire and the inferred root cause turns a confusing flurry into an actionable diagnosis.
body: Finding the cause in the cascade

When a fault cascades, the alarm that matters is usually the first one — the initiating event — but it is instantly buried under its consequences. First-out logic captures and preserves that initiating alarm, and root-cause presentation infers and foregrounds the underlying cause, so the operator diagnoses instead of firefighting symptoms. This is the diagnostic complement to flood suppression: suppression makes the list readable, root-cause makes it meaningful.

At the onset of a cascade, the system latches the first alarm in the causal sequence and marks it distinctly. Even as dozens of downstream alarms follow, the operator can see what started it. For the breeder, the first-out might be a specific stability-margin breach that preceded the disruption cascade; for the burner, a plug-density drop that preceded the confinement and DEC alarms. Knowing the initiator is what makes the response correct rather than merely reactive.

Beyond the first alarm, the twin's causal structure and the anomaly ensembles infer the most likely root cause and present it as a header over the collapsed cascade, with the evidence that supports it and a confidence. Because inference can be wrong, the root-cause header always shows its confidence and lets the operator expand the full evidence and override the diagnosis. It is a hypothesis offered with support, not a verdict imposed.
First-out: the latched initiating alarm, always preserved and highlighted
Root cause: inferred underlying cause with evidence and confidence
Cascade: collapsed under the cause, fully expandable, nothing discarded
Override: the operator can reject the inferred cause and see the raw sequence

First-out and root-cause presentation build on flood suppression and the precursor timeline, and every cascade is preserved intact for incident replay so the inferred cause can be checked against what actually happened.

title: From Decision to Experience: How L6 Consumes the Stack
lede: How Layer 6 draws from L1-L5 and where it deliberately holds no authority — the contract that lets observability be everywhere while control stays concentrated.
body: L6 is a consumer, not an authority

Layer 6 sits at the top of the KRONOS stack and depends on every layer beneath it, yet it deliberately holds no physics and no actuation authority. It consumes the outputs of L1-L5 and renders them for humans; it emits only advisory intents that flow back through the trust-and-override path. This clean separation — observability ubiquitous, authority concentrated in L1 — is what lets Kronos put the full picture on a phone without ever putting the machine at risk.
What L6 consumes from each layer
interlock/failsafe status, actuation state, real-time bounds
validated telemetry, timestamps, diagnostic health, lineage
job/pipeline status, model versions in effect

The latency gradient across the stack shows exactly why L6 is where it is: L1 runs microsecond hard-real-time loops, L3 the 1-100 ms twin, and L6 the 0.5 s-to-minutes human loop. L6 must never pretend to be faster than it is — hence the honest staleness and latency indicators — and must never insert itself into the fast paths it renders. It shows the fast world; it does not run it.

Everything an operator sees is traceable to a layer below, timestamped, confidence-scored, and provenance-tagged; everything an operator does is advisory, attributed, recorded, and overridable — with the L1 hardware failsafe always authoritative underneath. That contract is what makes the interface trustworthy enough to lean on and safe enough that leaning on it can never bypass the machine's own protections.

This overview ties the L6 pages together: the surfaces (overlay, dashboards, triage), the trust machinery (uncertainty, provenance, override), and the human-factors discipline (cognitive load) all serve the same contract, for both the breeder and the burner.
